opus-5.5.text:
I think "world model" has become one of those terms that everyone uses but people mean quite different things by it, so let me first say how I think about it.

To me, a world model is fundamentally an internal representation that lets a system predict, reason about, and act within an environment. It isn't just about generating pretty pixels. A lot of people see a video generation model produce a realistic clip and say, "Oh, that's a world model." But generation by itself doesn't mean you understand the world. You can produce something that looks plausible frame by frame without having any consistent notion of objects, physics, causality, or what happens if you intervene.

So I'd separate two things. One is the generative side: can you render the world, can you produce observations? The other is the representational side: do you have an abstract, structured understanding that supports prediction and planning? I think the second is the core of a world model, and the first is more like an output interface. Humans are a good example. Most of us can't paint a photorealistic scene, but we have a very strong world model. We know if I push this cup it will fall, we know a person who walks behind a wall still exists. That's understanding without high-fidelity generation.

Where it gets interesting is how understanding and generation interact. For a long time, vision research treated them as separate tracks: recognition models on one side, generative models on the other. I think the field is now realizing they need to be unified, and that good representations are what connects them. If your generative model is built on top of strong visual representations, it learns faster and generalizes better. In the other direction, generative objectives can push a model to capture more of the structure in the data. So the world model, in a sense, is the shared substrate that both understanding and generation should draw from.

Another point I care about is that language alone is not enough. Large language models have learned an enormous amount about the world through text, but text is a compressed, human-filtered description of reality. A lot of what matters—spatial relationships, physical dynamics, the continuous nature of how things change—is very hard to fully capture in language. So if we want AI systems that truly operate in the physical world, whether that's robotics or embodied agents or even just really grounded multimodal assistants, we need models that learn from sensory experience, especially vision, and build their own understanding from it.

Finally, I'd say a real world model should be useful for action. The test isn't "does the output look good," it's "can an agent use this model to imagine consequences and make better decisions?" That's a much harder bar, and honestly I think we're still early. But that's what makes it one of the most exciting directions right now. It pulls together representation learning, generative modeling, and embodied intelligence into one question: how does a machine come to understand the world it lives in?

r001.rationale: It says rendering observations is an output interface, while the core world model is the structured representation that supports understanding and planning.

r002.rationale: It describes what a world model is and what it should enable, but does not characterize it as a goal rather than a particular algorithm or technical route.

r003.rationale: It explicitly calls the world model a shared substrate from which understanding and generation should draw.

r004.rationale: It does not claim that upper-layer decoding becomes simple once the world model is sufficiently capable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, a world model is really the piece that sits between perception and generation. For a long time these two directions in computer vision were kind of separate communities. You had people working on understanding, recognition, representation learning, and then you had people working on generation, GANs, diffusion models, and so on. And I always felt that was a bit artificial, because if you look at how humans work, understanding and generation are deeply intertwined. You can't really imagine something without having some internal model of how the world behaves, and you can't really understand a scene without being able to predict, at least roughly, what happens next.

So to me, a world model is an internal representation that captures the structure of the world, the physics, the object permanence, the causal relationships, the way things move and interact. And the important point is that this representation should be useful in both directions. On the understanding side, it lets a system reason about what it's seeing, not just label it. On the generation side, it constrains what the model produces so that the output is actually consistent and plausible, rather than just visually pretty.

I think right now a lot of video generation models are, in a sense, learning world models implicitly. When you train a model to predict future frames at scale, it has to pick up on things like gravity, occlusion, how liquids behave. But whether that implicit knowledge is actually accessible, whether you can read it out and use it for planning or reasoning, that's still a very open question. My own view is that we should be more intentional about it. Rather than hoping a good world model emerges as a byproduct of generation, we should be thinking about what representations we want the model to have, and how we evaluate whether it really understands the world or is just interpolating in pixel space.

And this is also where I get a bit cautious about the language model analogy. People sometimes assume that if you scale up next-token prediction on video, you get a world model for free. Maybe. But vision is different from language in some fundamental ways. Language is already a compressed, human-structured abstraction. Pixels are not. So I think the representation question, what is the right intermediate space for a world model to live in, is actually the central problem, and it's one that connects understanding and generation rather than keeping them apart.

r001.rationale: The response describes a world model as an internal representation and says it constrains generation, but does not characterize human-facing outputs as its interface.

r002.rationale: The response discusses what a world model should represent and support, but does not frame it as a goal rather than an algorithm or technical route.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the representation should be useful for both understanding and generation, presenting the world model as their shared foundation.

r004.rationale: The response does not claim that upper-layer decoding becomes simple when a world model is sufficiently capable.

astra-6.text:
I think a world model is an internal model of how the world works. It’s more than recognizing what’s in an image or generating something that looks plausible. It should capture relationships: how objects interact, how a scene changes over time, and what might happen if you take a particular action.

That connects understanding and generation. If a system understands a situation, generating possible futures is one way to express—and test—that understanding. But a convincing image or video doesn’t automatically mean the system has learned the underlying rules. It might produce something visually beautiful and still get a simple physical interaction wrong.

So I would think of a world model as a foundation for prediction and, eventually, planning. The important question is whether the model can use what it has learned to handle a new situation: predict consequences, account for uncertainty, and update its predictions when new information arrives. That’s a stronger requirement than simply producing realistic content.

r002.rationale: It frames the world model in terms of desired capabilities—capturing relationships, predicting consequences, and supporting planning—without prescribing a particular algorithm or technical route.

r003.rationale: It connects understanding and generation, describing generated futures as a way to express and test understanding, with the world model as their basis.

r004.rationale: The response does not claim that upper-layer decoding becomes simple once the world model is capable enough.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a world model is an internal understanding of how the world works. It goes beyond recognizing what is in an image or producing something that looks plausible. It captures relationships: how objects interact, how a scene changes over time, and what might happen if you take a particular action.

Understanding and generation are closely connected here. If a system really understands a situation, it should be able to predict possible outcomes. And generating those outcomes can help us examine what the system has actually learned. But a convincing image or video alone doesn’t establish that it understands the underlying physics or causality.

For me, the interesting question is whether that representation can support prediction, reasoning, and action across different situations. Can the model handle something unfamiliar? Can it update its expectations when it gets new evidence? That’s where a world model becomes useful beyond content generation: it gives the system a basis for interacting with the world.
